body.p: Mary Mather was born in Perthshire, Scotland, in 1821, but she did not marry until 1852 (age 31) in Glasgow. By that time her younger sister Elizabeth had a two-year-old son, and the two women and baby John sailed from Glasgow to Melbourne together on the Sophia Burbidge in 1853. Elizabeth’s husband, James Hiddle, was already in Melbourne, and they went on to have another six children, but Mary had none. Her husband, George Mather, was lodging with Elizabeth and James in Glasgow at the time of the 1851 Scotland Census, but his emigration and death do not appear in Victoria’s records.

Nevertheless, despite her husband not appearing in the story, Mary was described as ‘a married woman’ after being subjected to a frightening attack by a drunken man at Christmas time in 1854. She told the court ‘with a volubility peculiar to a few of her sex’, that the man ‘had thrown at her chamber window “in the dead waste and middle of the night,” a pretty considerable length of an iron bar’. The iron bar was produced in court, and the man’s solicitor did not dispute that he had ‘used very threatening language towards her’, but he pleaded that his defendant was drunk. The court could therefore be assured, the solicitor said, that his client ‘was not in earnest with regard to the threats’. The magistrates responded to this plea by simply binding the man him over to keep the peace for six months. Whether he did so, and whether he and a friend paid the £25 sureties as required is not recorded. (The Argus 27 Dec 1854 p.5)

George Mather may have been absent when his wife was attacked in 1854, but a man of that name appears in the Melbourne directories in the early 1860s, and became a stall holder in the Eastern Market selling poultry in 1865 (Sands & McDougall 1865 p.315). Mrs Mather turned up the same year at 81 Cardigan St, Carlton (Sands & McDougall 1865 p.315), and purchased the newly-built house on the north-west corner of Pelham and Barry streets on her own account in 1867 (MCC Smith Ward Rates 105 1868). In 1873 she obtained a licence for the Pelham Hotel on the site (The Herald 16 September 1873 p.3), and advertised ‘Comfortable furnished Bedrooms. Board optional’ for ‘gentlemen and families’ (The Argus 11 Nov 1874 p.8). She was aiming for a genteel clientele drawn by the hotel’s proximity to the university, but in 1879 a mob of larrikins shattered the peace.

On a Tuesday evening in July six young men entered the hotel and demanded alcohol (The Argus 13 July 1879 p.1). They were already ‘more or less intoxicated’, so (the newspapers reported) ‘the landlady properly refused to serve them’. That led to violence. They took over the bar, ‘wasted a large quantity of the stock’, and when Mrs Mather ordered them to leave she was ‘struck upon the head with a bottle, which inflicted a somewhat severe scalp wound’. The police and a bystander were also badly treated in the course of arresting four of the men (Weekly Times 6 Sept 1879 p.14).

In the 1880s the Pelham Hotel became a landmark for advertisers: ‘apply two doors from Pelham hotel’ or ‘opposite Pelham Hotel’ or ‘back of Pelham Hotel’. By 1888 Mary Mather’s confidence was high enough to take out a mortgage on the hotel and buy the house next door (PROV VPRS 28/P0 Mary Mather, 45/725; MCC Smith Ward rates 196 & 197 1888 and 195 & 196 1889). The hotel had twelve bedrooms with a bath and a cellar, and there were another six bedrooms in the house next door, but she rented the new house out while the man who was probably her husband was living in a boarding house not far away, at 37 Barkly Street (PROV VPRS 28/P2 Mary Mather 45/725; George Mather, Sands & McDougall 1876 p.478 to after 1885 p.719). In 1889 Mrs Mather was trusted with the widely-advertised annual dinner of the Victoria Bowling Club, but early in 1890 she leased the hotel to a newcomer, transferred her publican’s license to him, and went to live with one of her sister Elizabeth’s children in Moonee Ponds (The Age 6 Feb 1890 p.6). She died the following year (The Argus 21 May 1891 p.1, VIC death 1891/6009). Her estate was valued at £3,300, and was divided between her five nieces and nephews. Her sister lived another twenty years, dying at Williamstown in 1913, the oldest member of the Williamstown Presbyterian Church, and ‘noted for her kindly disposition’ (Williamstown Chronicle, 25 October 1913, p.2).
